claim: A preregistered metastudy of 159 interaction hypotheses from 82 recent psychology articles found the overall median statistical power to detect a typical-size interaction was .18.
stance_target: published psychology interaction tests are systematically underpowered
scope_conditions: 159 studies (194 interaction hypotheses) from 82 articles across 10 influential psychology journals, published 2017-2021
quoted_support: The overall median power to detect interactions of a typical size is .18. ... Overall, only 17% of the studies had a power at or above .80, and the median power was .18
entities: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

claim: Median statistical power to detect the hypothesized interaction varied sharply by interaction shape: .87 for reversed interactions, .36 for fully attenuated interactions, and .11 for partially attenuated interactions.
stance_target: interaction shape strongly moderates statistical power in practice
scope_conditions: Subsamples of the 159-study metastudy: n=23 reversed, n=54 fully attenuated, n=74 partially attenuated
quoted_support: the power to detect a +0.35 |−0.35 reversed interaction was at or above .80 in 65% of the cases, and the median power was = .87. ... the power to detect a +0.35|0.00 fully attenuated interaction was at or above .80 in 19% of the cases, and the median power was .36. ... the power to detect a +0.35|+0.20 (or, equivalently, a +0.35|+0.50) partially attenuated interaction was at or above .80 in none of the cases, and the median power was .11.

claim: Only 4% of the 159 studies in the metastudy reported an adequate (shape-aware) power analysis for their interaction hypothesis; 45% reported no power analysis at all.
stance_target: researchers rarely conduct correct power analyses for interaction effects
quoted_support: Less than 5% of the studies used an adequate power analysis. Out of the 159 studies, 45% did not report a power/sensitivity analysis—specifically, 65 did not report any analysis, three did not specify the type of analysis, and three reported an incorrect “post hoc” power analysis

claim: Achieving sufficient power to detect interactions is inherently harder than for main effects because interaction effect sizes are typically small, requiring much larger samples, a point also made in Gelman's (2018) '16 times the sample size' rule of thumb cited by the authors.
stance_target: interactions require larger samples / are harder to detect than main effects
scope_conditions: General statistical power theory for two-way (first-order) interactions vs. main effects, applies to between-participants designs with dichotomous or continuous predictors
quoted_support: achieving sufficient power to detect interactions is not an easy task because either the effect size of interactions is often small and, by extension, the required sample size is often very large (Brysbaert, 2019). This can prevent scholars with limited resources ... from achieving adequate power. Although there has been much discussion about the issue of statistical power for interactions in popular blogs (Gelman, 2018; Giner-Sorolla, 2018; Simonsohn, 2014)
numbers: 16x (cited Gelman 2018 blog title: 'You need 16 times the sample size to estimate an interaction than to estimate a main effect')

claim: Conducting an appropriate power analysis for interactions cannot be easily done with standard software (e.g., G*Power, pwr package) because the expected effect size of an interaction depends on its shape, unlike main-effect power analysis.
stance_target: interaction power analysis requires shape-specific methodology beyond standard tools
quoted_support: conducting appropriate power analysis for interactions cannot be easily carried out with software such as G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) or packages such as pwr (Champely et al., 2017) because the expected effect size of an interaction depends on its shape (Maxwell & Delaney, 2004). This can lead scholars to base their power analyses on an incorrect effect size.

claim: The authors developed three preregisterable methods to increase statistical power for detecting interactions without increasing sample size: one-tailed tests (+21% power gain), mixed within/between designs (+75% gain), and contrast analysis for fully attenuated interactions (+62% gain), validated via ~900 million simulated data sets.
stance_target: methods to raise power for interaction tests without larger N
scope_conditions: Simulation study covering 12 interaction types (shape x simple-slope-size taxonomy)
quoted_support: we use simulations (≈900,000,000 data sets) to generate power curves for the 12 types of interactions and test three approaches to increase power without increasing sample size: (a) preregistering one-tailed tests (+21% gain), (b) using a mixed design (+75% gain), and (c) preregistering contrast analysis for a fully attenuated interaction (+62% gain)

claim: If focusing on larger versions of hypothesized interactions, the proportion of adequately powered studies rises to 27% and the median power rises to .25, still far below conventional .80 standard.
stance_target: underpowering of interaction tests is robust even under generous effect-size assumptions
scope_conditions: 159-study metastudy, sensitivity analysis using larger hypothesized effect sizes (+0.50|−0.50, +0.50|0.00, +0.50|+0.20)
quoted_support: If we repeat the analysis while focusing on larger versions of the hypothesized interactions (i.e., +0.50|−0.50, +0.50|0.00, and +0.50|+0.20), 27% of the studies had a power at or above .80, and the median power was .25.
